Twyne UX improvement brief
Discussion notes and proposed product directionKeith Noel • October 19, 2026
Twyne needs to make its editorial work visible, explain why its feedback matters, and connect that feedback to the passages a writer can act on. This brief consolidates the observations and suggestions from our discussion about cast replies, passage relationships, editor reviews, automatic research, and manuscript versions.
The guiding principle is that every card should help the writer make a recognizable writing decision. Prioritize reliable delivery of review and research results, then develop richer passage and revision views.
What was observed
Cast or persona response cards sometimes quote several manuscript passages, but currently appear to link only to one region or the initial quotation.
A visually appealing view connects passages A and B without clearly explaining why they are connected or what the writer should do with that relationship. The exact name and purpose of the “further on as you read” card remain uncertain.
Editor feedback requested from the rubric initially appeared absent. Later in the same session, responses did appear, but discovering them required a manual click. This changes the diagnosis: delivery and visibility are established concerns; a generation failure was not established.
The apparatus or automatic research area appeared to remain at “watching graph,” without visible research findings. This does not establish whether background research actually ran.
Manual checks appeared to run, although the tools felt inconsistent. The editorial board version page offered checkpoint restoration and revision tasks, but its words and passages before-and-after bars did not communicate useful revision insight.
How to read this brief
Observations reflect the walkthrough, not an independent code or runtime audit. Proposed behavior captures the improvements discussed. Completion criteria below translate those proposals into reviewable outcomes; they are not claims about implemented functionality. “Jev” refers to the type-safe System One decision model or system, including the transcription variants GEV and Jeb.

Passage links and meaningful feedback
Link every quotation to its source
Each quoted manuscript passage inside a cast reply should have its own connection to the corresponding source passage. A response discussing several passages must support several links, rather than sending every quotation to the first anchor.
The discussion began with Jev identifying quotations in the response, then moved toward deterministic matching because literal quotations should already exist in the manuscript. Use direct text matching where possible. Model judgment is useful when interpretation is needed, but is unnecessary for an unambiguous exact quote.
Make each resolved quote clickable. Activating it should jump to and highlight its own manuscript passage.
Use surrounding context to distinguish repeated phrases. Matching the same words in two places is not enough to identify the intended source.
As an implementation safeguard, leave uncertain or unmatched quotations unresolved rather than silently assigning an incorrect passage. Revalidate links when edits change the source text.
Explain why passages are related
Preserve the useful visual connection between passages, but add a plain explanation of the relationship and its writing consequence. Showing two excerpts alone leaves the writer to infer the purpose of the card.
Possible relationship labels discussed were an unpaid promise, a conflict, or an echo. Pair the label with a specific explanation: for example, an earlier passage introduces an expectation that the later passage has not yet addressed. These are illustrative categories, not confirmed names of current features.
Show why these particular passages were selected and what question or revision the connection raises.
Let the writer agree with the interpretation or push back. A relationship is an editorial reading, not automatically a defect.
Inspect the existing “further on as you read” feature before deciding whether its presentation, name, or underlying function needs to change.
Protect author intent and remember decisions
Let writers tell the editors what they intend to preserve, so feedback does not erase an intentional stylistic or structural choice. Give feedback memory: the writer should be able to mark a note “intentional” or “later” and avoid receiving the same note repeatedly unless the relevant text changes.
Completion criteria
A response containing three distinct quotations can navigate to all three intended passages. Repeated phrases do not silently point to the wrong occurrence. Each relationship card explains its editorial relevance, and dismissed or deferred feedback respects the writer’s recorded decision.

Editor reviews and automatic research
Make requested reviews visible
The later appearance of editor replies is a crucial correction to the initial report of no response. The immediate issue is that the writer could not tell what was happening and had to click to uncover the result. Investigate generation timing separately from notification and display behavior.
After a review request, show that reviewing is in progress. When it finishes, clearly show that feedback is ready and identify the editor speaking.
If the writer remains in the relevant panel, display the returned feedback automatically. If the writer moves away, use a quiet unread indicator that leads directly to it.
As a completion safeguard, distinguish a finished review with no findings from a pending review or an error; none should look like unexplained silence.
Give Jev a clear editorial role
Jev should help decide when proactive reviews are useful and which editor is relevant to the current text or situation. The walkthrough did not make this selection behavior apparent. The proposed separation is to use Jev for relevance and prioritization while treating delivery of explicitly requested feedback as dependable application behavior.
This means the writer should be able to understand who is responding and why that editor is useful. A requested review should not remain hidden merely because a separate prioritization decision has not surfaced it.
Make automatic research produce an outcome
The apparatus felt severely underdeveloped because “watching graph” did not lead to visible findings. The next investigation should determine whether the missing outcome comes from triggering, execution, or presentation. The discussion does not establish which layer is responsible.
Center the research experience on a claim in the manuscript. Show sources that support it, challenge it, or leave it unresolved, and explain what that evidence means for the wording or credibility of the passage. The writer needs findings or a clear reason that no useful result is available.
Connect research findings back to the claim or passage that prompted them.
Make the current state understandable: watching for relevant claims, researching, findings ready, or no useful result. Expose failures as actionable states rather than leaving the display at “watching graph.”
Treat the observation that manual checks run as a useful diagnostic lead, not proof that the automatic research path works.
Completion criteria
A requested editor review becomes visible without a discovery click when its panel is open, and has an unread indication when closed. Automatic research yields a claim-linked finding or an intelligible explanation of its outcome. A writer can distinguish waiting, completion, and failure.

Versions and delivery priorities
Organize versions around revision intent
The version page should help the writer understand what changed and decide whether the revision served its purpose. Word and passage totals can remain secondary metadata, but bars displaying counts alone do not explain the value or effect of an edit.
Lead with meaningful changes such as an opening rewritten, an argument moved, or a scene cut. Let the writer open the actual before-and-after passages for each change. These examples illustrate the desired level of explanation; they are not observed changes in a specific manuscript.
Keep checkpoint restoration available and easy to understand.
Visualize substantive revision information when it has actually been captured, instead of presenting counts as the main insight.
Connect revision tasks to the editor suggestions they address. Add a brief assessment of how the revision responds to the suggestion, while leaving the final judgment to the writer.
Make it possible to inspect the textual evidence behind any change summary or assessment.
Completion criteria
Given two checkpoints, the writer can identify a meaningful revision, inspect the corresponding before-and-after text, and understand its relationship to an editorial task where one exists. Restoration remains accessible. Counts provide context without dominating the page.
Proposed order of work
1. Stabilize editor feedback delivery and automatic research outcomes. First make the application clearly return useful work, explain its state, and expose the difference between no result and a failed operation.
2. Improve passage grounding and card meaning. Resolve every quotation, explain passage relationships, and make feedback respond to author intent and recorded decisions.
3. Develop the richer version experience. Build on reliable passage links and feedback to explain revisions, show evidence, and connect changes to editorial goals.
Questions to resolve during implementation
What are the exact component names and intended purposes of the cast cards and the “further on as you read” view?
Did the editor review finish before the manual click, or did that click initiate or refresh the result? What state was visible while waiting?
What triggers automatic research, and where does the path stop when only “watching graph” is shown?
Which editor-selection and review-timing decisions are already made by Jev, and how are those decisions surfaced?
What revision information is currently captured beyond word and passage counts, and can it support trustworthy explanations of changes?

content.text:
I've worked through all three parts of the brief in its suggested order. Typecheck and lint are clean, and the 129 tests in the files I touched pass (16 of them new). I haven't run the full test suite or checked any of this in the browser. Nothing is committed.

## 1. Editor feedback and research now report what's happening
- **Editor review in the rubric:** the Editors tab used to show "0" after a quick grade. That looked like the feedback was missing, but the quick check never asks the editors at all. The tab now says "not asked", or "reading…" while a run is in progress, and the empty panel explains why. This answers the brief's question about the manual click: the click *started* the review, nothing had been waiting.
- **Research no longer just says "watching":** the research module went quietly idle in five different situations. It now records which one and shows a plain sentence for it in both the side panel and the Apparatus page:
  - the draft is too short
  - no AI provider is set
  - it found no claims needing a source
  - every claim is already covered
  - the pass finished
- **Each research claim** now says what its result means. "No match" means the search ran and found nothing. "Failed" means the search broke, which is different from an empty result, and can be retried. Each claim also has a "Go to the claim" link.

## 2. Quotes link to their passages, and cards explain themselves
- **Every quote in an editor's note is clickable** (`src/utils/quote-grounding.ts`). This works in the note itself, in replies, and in the note that opens inside the manuscript. Matching is plain text matching that ignores quote styles, case and spacing, and handles quotes with "…" cut out of them. When a phrase appears more than once, the words around the quote in the note pick which one; a tie stays unresolved. A quote that can't be placed gets a dotted underline that says why. Links are re-checked whenever the draft changes, and again at the moment of the click.
- **"Further on in this piece" cards** now name the relationship: unpaid promise, tension, echo, repetition or same subject. Each comes with a one-line explanation, a view of both passages, and two buttons: "That's the connection" and "Not how I read it". If Jev decides two passages only share vocabulary, the card isn't shown at all.
- **"Intentional" and "later" buttons on each note.** That editor won't raise the same passage again until its text changes. The decisions are also passed to the editors as context, and settled notes are shown faded.

## 3. Version history
- Each checkpoint can record what the revision was for, and that intent is shown alongside it.
- Changes are labelled "Rewritten", "Cut" or "New passage", with the before and after text.
- If a change rewrote a passage an editor had commented on, that note appears beside it. The wording says it touched the note, not that it answered it.
- Word and passage counts are now folded into a "Size of the change" section you can expand. Restore works as before.

## Not done, and things to check
- **Unread markers for finished reviews**, from the completion criteria, aren't built.
- **Relationship labels come from an extra Jev question** added to the existing echo check. Cards created before this change, or when Jev can't be reached, fall back to "Shared words" with an explanation that nothing has read them for meaning.
- **"Not how I read it" just hides the card** using the existing dismiss. Nothing records that reading as rejected.
- **"Intentional" and "later" decisions are saved only in this browser**, keyed per document. They don't sync to Convex.

A source-check test had the old rendering call hard-coded, so I updated `personas-markdown-wiring.test.ts` to match.

input.content:
---
name: autonomy-by-default
description: Twyne should act on its own by default — reviews, research, editor readings run without the writer clicking; buttons are optional overrides
metadata:
  type: feedback
---

Twyne's default is autonomous, fluid action: editors read, research runs, reviews complete, and results arrive without the writer having to press a button. Manual controls may exist as options (re-run, steer, decline), but a feature that waits for a click before doing its core job is a design defect.

**Why:** The user (Keith Noel's product direction, restated by the owner 2026-10-20) said "waiting for the user to click a button is not what I want for this app… the default is autonomous fluid action."

**How to apply:** When building or fixing a feature, ask "does this happen if the writer never clicks?" If not, add an automatic trigger (on draft change / idle / panel open / folio open) with spend guards (dedupe per draft fingerprint, rate floors, session caps) rather than a call-to-action button. Empty states should say what the app is about to do on its own, not invite a click. Hosted (non-BYOK) users must get the autonomous path too. Related: [[skip-long-verification]].

content.text:
Twyne's default is now to act on its own. Typecheck and lint are clean and the 125 tests in the touched files pass (including 6 new ones). I haven't run the full suite or watched any of this happen in the browser, and nothing is committed.

## What now happens without a click

- **Editors read a draft as soon as it opens.** Before, any text already in a document counted as "already read", so the editors never commented on a draft until you clicked Get notes. Now Twyne remembers, per document, what the editors last read. A document they've never seen is read on its own once it reaches 500 words and you pause. Documents that already have notes stay quiet when reopened.
- **Rewrites trigger a reading, not just new text.** It used to take 500 *net new* words plus a 2-minute pause, so tightening or reworking prose never woke the editors. Now 200 new or rewritten words plus a 1-minute pause triggers a reading. The existing limits stay: at least 5 minutes between readings and at most 8 per session.
- **Research works without your own AI model.** Before, a signed-in writer with no model configured got no automatic research at all. Now Twyne picks out likely claims from the text itself (figures, quotations, "studies show", dated events), Jev confirms which really need a source, and the search runs through Twyne's service. Fiction is handled differently, so made-up events don't get researched. This is in `src/utils/research-candidates.ts`.
- **Failed research retries itself.** A failed pass or claim is tried again after 30 seconds, then 2 minutes, then 10 minutes. After that it stops and the retry button stays on screen.
- **The editors' reading in the rubric runs on its own.** When a new quick grade arrives for a version the editors haven't read, they read it in the background, at most every 10 minutes, and the grade stays visible meanwhile. Their notes no longer disappear when the next quick grade refreshes. If you keep typing during their reading, the notes are kept and marked as being on an earlier version.
- **Versions describe themselves.** Every comparison now gets a sentence like "Rewrote 3 passages and cut 1. The changes reach passages Marrow had notes on." The "what was this revision for" field is now optional.

The buttons are all still there (Get notes, Ask them now, Grade this draft, retry), but as shortcuts. Empty panels now say what Twyne is about to do instead of asking you to click. I updated the in-app manual's two passages about asking the editors to match.

## Decisions for you

- **Cost.** These changes spend more model calls than before. Editors can read up to 8 times per session, the rubric reading up to 6 times an hour, and hosted research makes one batched Jev call per pass. The limits are constants in `background-room.ts`, `rubric-panel.tsx` (`ROOM_READ_FLOOR_MS`) and `background-research.ts`.
- **Automatic rubric readings save versions less often.** A reading you ask for still always saves a checkpoint. One the editors start themselves follows the same 5-minute spacing as automatic checkpoints, so they can't push your own checkpoints out of the 50-version history.
- **Some things deliberately stay manual:** inserting citations into the manuscript, Propose edits, and the full-page analysis. These either change your text or are a deeper on-demand view.

I also saved "autonomous by default" as a standing preference for future work on Twyne.

# Twyne documentation

A guide to using the writing room, understanding its data, and maintaining the app.

**For writers:** open [The Manual](https://www.twyne.love/docs/) in Twyne. It covers
the desk, the House, conversations in the margin, source and proof, and shortcuts.
Numbered visual walkthroughs show the actual controls, with editor illustrations
and optional films at the beginning of relevant chapters. The contents panel
follows your current chapter and shows your reading position as you scroll.

**For contributors:** start with the [project README](../README.md#development),
then follow the guide for the part you are changing.

## The writing room

| Guide                                                 | Use it for                                                                          |
| ----------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [The House and the fluid desk](flow-and-context.md)   | Context inheritance, focus, margin conversations and their storage contract.        |
| [Live voice](live-voice.md)                           | Voice sessions, the relay and conversation limits.                                  |
| [Publishing from Twyne](publishing-from-twyne.md)     | Writer-owned PDS publishing and public reading pages.                               |
| [Not Organic identity](notorganic-native-identity.md) | The account boundary and native sign-in design.                                     |
| [Launch film](launch-film.md)                         | The bilingual introduction, contextual chapter films and visual walkthrough assets. |

## Running and maintaining Twyne

| Guide                                                       | Use it for                                                     |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- |
| [Deployment](DEPLOYMENT.md)                                 | Railway, environment variables, domains and the desktop build. |
| [Data and sync architecture](architecture/data-and-sync.md) | The recorded storage/sync architecture and its dated findings. |
| [Internationalisation](i18n.md)                             | Locale selection, translation and preparation commands.        |
| [AI observability](ai-observability.md)                     | Traces, experiments and editorial evaluation.                  |
| [Popmelt integration](popmelt.md)                           | The recorded capture and interaction integration.              |

## Design and implementation records

These describe intent and implementation history. A plan is not evidence that a
feature is deployed or that its provider integration has been exercised.

that draft, Salt Roads, from a brief to a proof.

Twyne is a writing desk with an editorial room attached. You write on the page. A small cast of editors reads in the margin, each with a different job, and nothing they say changes a word until you say so. Three habits make the room worth having:

  1. Say what the piece is for. The{" "} dossier holds the reader, the goal and the shape of the piece. Editors with a brief give better notes than editors guessing.
  2. Write first, read notes later. Your draft saves on this device as you type.{" "} The margin holds feedback beside the passage it belongs to, and waits until you look up.
  3. Revise on your own terms. Follow a note to its passage, argue with it, ask a different editor, or check the galley proof. Every change is yours to make or refuse.

Go to the writing desk →

02 · At the desk

The dossier

Morgan's first draft of Salt Roads was beautiful and pointless. The dossier is where you admit what a piece is supposed to do, so the editors can tell you whether it does it.

Before the room opens, it asks a short series of questions. They feel like paperwork and they are the opposite: a dossier is the difference between an editor saying "this paragraph is weak" and an editor saying "this paragraph loses the reader you said you were writing for." Answer briefly and honestly. You can change any answer later.

Ten sections, and what each is really asking:

  • Working title. A name the room can use. It does not have to be the final one.
  • Form. Essay, memo, chapter, dispatch, proposal. The shape sets expectations about length and

04 · At the desk

Writing in flow

Morgan writes in long runs and resents anything that interrupts one. The room is built to wait.

While you work, Twyne can bring comments, sources, books, records and echoes of your earlier writing into the margin, each beside the passage it concerns. Nothing pops up over the page. Hover or focus a marker to see what it connects to; select it to open the conversation in the same margin.

A quieter page

Automatic focus reads your typing cadence. When you have been writing steadily for a while, it quiets the room: new cards wait, controls recede, and the page is the only thing left. Pause, or reach for the room, and it comes back. You can also enter focus yourself with Zen in the manuscript status bar, and leave it with Esc.

Help when you need it

When a passage stalls, the margin may offer a single connection or a short way into the next sentence. These are offers, not corrections; ignore them and they go away. If what you are writing drifts from the dossier, the room may propose an amendment. It never rewrites the brief behind your back.

Your controls: Automatic review, margin tools, automatic focus and cover lookups each have their own switch in the review controls. The desk learns your timing and preferences on this device. Cover lookups are the one feature here that talks to the outside world: they send book or record titles to external catalogues.

05 · At the desk

The piece

Some problems only show up across the whole draft: the voice that shifts, the name spelled two ways, the character who vanishes for a chapter.

Useful without a model

The piece runs on this device, with no model and no cost. It watches first-person stance, similar names, and the conventions your draft mostly follows: spelling, small numbers, quotation marks, dashes and list punctuation. It also maps where each recurring name appears across the headed sections. A finding is a pattern worth a look. Whether it is a problem is your call.

Choose Stance, Names, Style or Presence to see that lens on the page. Open a finding for its passages and the actions it offers. On a narrow screen the desk sits below the writing area, and Close gives the space back to the draft. Zen hides it while you write.

Know what the score means

The ≈ sign marks an estimate. Consistency can move as you revise, because local rules re-count; that movement is not a new editorial opinion. Score details separates the measures made by rule from those made by review. An overall estimate appears at about 150 words.

Confirm with a full read asks for a fresh editorial reading of the current draft. It needs automatic review switched on, at least 500 words, and a signed-in model service. The desk says so when a request cannot run. Edit again afterwards and the score becomes an estimate until the new draft has been read.

Your choices stay yours. Fixes change only the listed passages, and Undo reverses them. A deliberate exception stays with the folio on this device. Above 80,000 characters the desk pauses these checks and asks you to divide the work into folios.

06 · At the desk

Writing instruments

A sentence that is almost right. A paragraph that sounds like one you wrote earlier. A scene with no sound in it. Each gets a tool that opens beside the words, not instead of them.

Select text in the manuscript and the tools that fit it appear. A single word offers Alternatives. A passage offers Rework, with Hear it read, Threads, Scene bench and Task desk under More. The Compositor also opens Task desk from Review. Close a tool, or press Escape, and the page is back.

07 · The editorial room

Your editors

Five resident voices, each reading for something different. No single editor is right about everything, which is rather the point of having five.

You will come to know them by their faces. The same portraits accompany each editor's critiques, margin replies and rubric readings, so a glance tells you whether it was the sceptic or the copy chief who objected. A custom editor without a portrait signs with their initials. From any writing instrument, Ask the room brings one of them into the question you are already working on.

Arrange your room

Custom editors: Visit{" "} the Room of Editors {" "} to add, edit or reorder the cast. An editor needs a name, a role and a description of how they talk; the more specific the description, the more consistently the model stays in character. Morgan's Route Reader exists because nobody else in the room cared about distances.

Changing the model

Each editor is only as good as the model reading for them. A careful, precise model makes Mlle. Sceptique sharper. A warmer one makes Sœur Encourageante more generous. In{" "} Preferences {" "} you can assign different models to different jobs, and the room adapts.

08 · The editorial room

The galley proof

Salt Roads got a B. That is not information. The reasons under the grade are.

The static features are the part of the proof that never guesses: sentence length distribution, type-token ratio, citation density, paragraph shape. They are computed on this device, cost nothing and call nothing. They give you a cold, honest picture of the draft's mechanics, and nothing at all about whether it is any good.

Quick check

When the signed-in service is available, the default check makes one typed judgement request against your enabled criteria, custom ones included. You get a grade without separate verdicts from the five editors. If the quick check is unavailable, Twyne falls back to the room reading.

The editors' reading

After a quick check, the editors read the new version on their own, at most once every ten minutes, and the grade stays on screen while they do. Choose Ask them now on the Editors tab if you would rather not wait. Each editor gives a score and a rationale, and the places where they disagree are usually where the revision is. This path combines editorial verdicts with the static features. Its Target Fit check caps the shape scores when a piece misses the audience or purpose in its dossier, because a beautifully built essay for the wrong reader is still the wrong essay.

What the letters mean:

  • A range. Publishable or nearly so. Polish.
  • B range. A solid draft with clear, fixable problems. This is where Salt Roads sits.
  • C range. Doing the work, but a real pass is still needed.
  • D to F range. The important next pass is still ahead.

Use the rationale, not the letter: read the explanation beside each criterion and hold it against your own purpose. The rubric is one more reading of the draft. You decide which of its complaints deserve a revision.

09 · The editorial room

Margin conversations

Every argument about a passage happens next to the passage. Your notes, the editors' notes, and the replies between them.

Select any passage and choose Comment to leave a note in the margin. Notes belong to the folio and travel with it. Each one can hold replies, and Ask an editor invites a particular voice into the thread when you want a second opinion on your own doubt.

Select a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve it there. One conversation is in the foreground at a time; on a narrow screen its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to close it. A reply you have not sent survives switching threads during the visit, but not a reload, so send it or lose it.

10 · The editorial room

Research & citations

The 1911 survey, the tide table, the book Morgan keeps paraphrasing. The Apparatus notices them and keeps them in order.

The Apparatus does three things: finds sources, keeps them, and cites them. As you write it recognises DOIs, URLs, ISBNs and author-year references in the text. You can also search by query; the panel returns a shortlist with title, author, publisher and a snippet. Save what matters to the bibliography and ignore the rest.

The bibliography is formatted in the style you choose, MLA, APA or Chicago, and switches instantly when an editor changes their mind. Copy the whole list to the clipboard in one go.

The full Apparatus lives at{" "} /apparatus . The citation tab in the right panel shows a quick view of what has been detected without leaving the page.

an account. See [the House and fluid desk guide](docs/flow-and-context.md) for
context inheritance, margin behavior and sync boundaries.

## The editorial room

The manuscript’s margins hold comments, editor notes, sources and connections.
Click a passage marker to unfold its conversation beside the draft. The **Cast**,
**Rubric**, **Marginalia** and **Apparatus** panels remain available for browsing;
their tabs show unread work. Automatic focus quiets the surrounding room during
sustained writing, with a manual override in the review controls.

### The room reads as you write

Convening the room is deliberate and expensive — five model calls over the
whole manuscript. Alongside it, a background pass runs on a narrower brief:
once you've written **~300 net new words** _and_ stopped typing for **two
minutes**, all five editors read **only the new paragraphs**, plus a digest of
how the draft has been moving.

Those arrive as quieter "in passing" notes in the Cast panel. Two spend guards
sit on top — a five-minute floor between passes and a per-session cap — because
this runs without you asking. Turn it off with **Read as I write** in the room
settings.

The same digest goes along when you _do_ press Convene, so the deliberate pass
knows the trajectory rather than re-reading a cold snapshot.

### The rubric grades against _this_ piece

The default signed-in check first attempts one typed judgement over the enabled
criteria, including custom criteria. **Ask the editors** runs the separate room
reading; Twyne also tries that path when the quick check is unavailable.

In the room reading, the static feature scorer measures shape — sentence-length variance,
type-token ratio, paragraph balance. It never reads the brief, so fluent prose
about the wrong subject used to score 10/10 on three categories.

That path’s **Target Fit** judge scores relevance independently of craft, and caps
every shape-derived criterion by it. Lowering target fit can only ever lower
the grade, never raise it.

The criteria themselves are yours to shape. Twyne ships a fixed spine so a
score in March means the same thing in June; you can disable or reweight any of
it, add criteria of your own ("stays in second person", "every section ends on
an image") for the room to judge, or ask it to **suggest criteria** fitted to
your format — proposals you accept, never applied silently. Customise anything

- Hovering or focusing a passage marker reveals its associated margin card and
  connections. Clicking a comment or persona note unfolds its full conversation
  in that margin slot. Suggestions use the same placement service.
- One conversation owns the foreground at a time. Switching preserves separate
  unsent reply drafts for the mounted editor session; reloading does not preserve
  those unsent drafts. Sent replies retain the existing storage behavior.
- On narrow screens or with automatic margin reading disabled, the existing
  anchored card provides the fallback. Ambient dock cards yield to open threads,
  tools and selection actions. Open margin cards adapt to viewport changes.
- Cards follow document scrolling and step around tools and expanded threads.
  Escape closes the active conversation. Selection actions yield while a thread
  or suggestion is open.
- Fallback comment, persona-note and suggestion cards follow their passage too.
  A passive listener on the manuscript scroller and resize/reflow updates share
  one animation frame. Cards without a margin slot tuck below or above the live
  passage; slot conversations keep the existing margin handshake. A passage fully
  outside the visible manuscript closes a fallback card without a pin or draft.
  Pinned notes and unsent drafts stay clamped on screen. Split marks count as
  visible while any fragment remains in view.
- Manual focus remains available. Automatic focus fades workspace chrome without
  collapsing the writer's side panels. Interacting with controls or a conversation
  prevents automatic focus from hiding them. A manual exit overrides automatic
  focus temporarily.

## Focus and assistance

`flow-state.ts` reads typing cadence; `flow-profile.ts` learns pause thresholds and
item preferences locally. Working shows a small selection, settling holds new
items, flow clears ambient cards, and stuck favors one relevant item plus its
connections. `flow-conductor.ts` combines these signals with budgeted Jev calls.
Local connections are candidates, not claims of semantic certainty. Drift checks
propose amendments rather than silently rewriting the dossier.

| Reading  | What the margin does                          |
| -------- | --------------------------------------------- |
| Working  | Offers a small selection of relevant items.   |
| Settling | Keeps existing items and holds new arrivals.  |

| Stuck    | Favors one relevant item and its connections. |

`FlowSnapshot.heldKinds` is the pneumatic post's tally: held items by kind, beside
the total `held`. It includes only policy-held items, including a waiting way in;
dismissed items do not count. The margin can name what is waiting without showing
the cards during a quiet run.

record titles go to MusicBrainz and covers come from the Cover Art Archive.

titles, dossier changes and model decisions: inspect an export before sharing it.

## Storage and sync

`house-store.ts` serializes local edits, verifies IndexedDB writes and emits
`twyne:house-changed`. Each edit advances the whole snapshot's timestamp, including
collection membership changes and withdrawals. House state sync runs on both the
House page and the editor, with a live Convex subscription and reconnect refresh.

House, collections and charter use the newer complete snapshot; this is
last-write-wins, not a per-field collaborative merge. Ledger entries are unioned
by ID. A stale server upload may contribute history but cannot replace a newer
snapshot. Local history retains 500 entries; server history is paginated. Signed-out
writing remains local. The current local House is shared within the browser profile,
as with the existing local folio store.

the server's bounded history window. An acknowledged entry is not uploaded again
just because it is absent from the latest pull. Partial uploads retry only the
unacknowledged batches; persisting an acknowledgement can retry without repeating

the editor mounts its full conversation, then receives geometry updates. Pending
reservations survive the old card closing. Editor request tokens prevent slower

# Dossier UX cleanup — change summary

A focused pass on the dossier refinery (`/dossier/refine`) and dossier onboarding (`/dossier/create`) to fix three related UX problems:

1. The mode switch (Form / Conversation) was hidden when the writer switched into conversation — only the form side rendered the toggle, so there was no way back without the overloaded "Cancel / Use form" button the conversation chrome was carrying.
2. Several different "close" / "cancel" / "back" buttons were scattered across the dossier routes (top-bar back link, form "Close", conversation "Cancel", and a "Close" on the drift-report panel). They meant different things and made it hard to know what any given click would do.
3. There was no way to start the dossier over from scratch on the refinery page. The only way to "redo" the brief was to either pick a different mode (which kept the answers) or re-onboard from scratch (which lost the manuscript).

## What changed

### 1. Shared top bar — `src/components/onboarding/dossier-top-bar.tsx` (new)

A single component that owns the page-level chrome for both dossier routes:

- **Back link** (left): "← Back to desk" on `/dossier/refine`, "← Back home" on `/dossier/create` (when no folio exists yet).
- **Start over** (refine only): destructive, opens a confirm dialog rather than acting directly.
- **Mode switch** (right): right-aligned Form / Conversation pills, same shape in both directions, persistent across both modes so the writer can always switch back.

### 2. Plumbed existing-brief carry-over through the conversation

`Start over` writes the current folio draft into `localStorage` under a one-shot `twyne-starting-material` slot and routes to `/dossier/create/`. The create route reads it on hydration, then clears it. Both authoring surfaces (form and conversation) now consume it:

- **Form** (`AntiTabulaRasa`): new `initialMaterial` prop seeds the form's existing-material field.
- **Conversation** (`ConversationalInterview`): new `initialMaterial` prop is plumbed into the interview-turn request as `startingMaterial` and forwarded to both the Convex `runInterviewTurn` action and the client-side `runClientInterviewTurn` wrapper. The interview system prompt receives a `--- BEGIN MANUSCRIPT ---` block when present, so the AI orients its first question around the writer's draft rather than rediscovering it from scratch.

### 3. Removed in-body exit buttons

- `AntiTabulaRasa`: dropped its in-body `Close` button and the `onCancel$` prop (the top bar is now the only exit).

# Autonomous editorial work — change summary

Responds to the Twyne UX improvement brief (Keith Noel, 2026-10-19,
[`Twyne_UX_Improvement_Brief.docx`](../Twyne_UX_Improvement_Brief.docx)) and to
the product direction that followed it: **Twyne acts without being asked.**
Reviews, research and editors' readings run on their own; buttons remain as
shortcuts and overrides, not as the way work starts.

Not yet released. Fold into `CHANGELOG.md` at the next version.

## Principle

A feature that waits for a click before doing its core job is a defect. Each
automatic path has a trigger (folio open, draft change, idle pause, a fresh
quick grade) and spend guards (rate floors, session caps, dedupe by draft
fingerprint). Empty states say what Twyne is about to do, not what to press.
Hosted writers without their own model get the automatic path too.

## 1. Review and research arrive on their own

### Background room — `src/utils/background-room.ts`

| Before                                                         | After                                                                                       |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Existing prose counted as read on every open, so an unread draft was never read until Get notes | What the room last read is stored per folio (`background-room-read:<folioId>`). A folio with no record and no notes starts empty and is read on its own; one with notes from before the record existed counts as read |
| Triggered by 500 **net** new words and a 2-minute pause         | Triggered by 200 words in new or rewritten paragraphs (`diffParagraphs(...).added`) and a 1-minute pause |
| `startBackgroundRoom` had no current draft                      | `currentText` arms the watcher straight away when the draft holds unread work               |

Guards unchanged: `MIN_INTERVAL_MS` (5 min), `MAX_PASSES_PER_SESSION` (8),
`MIN_EDITOR_WORDS` (500) before any reading. `src/routes/editor/index.tsx`
loads the stored baseline and existing notes when the folio opens.

### Rubric — `src/components/rubric/rubric-panel.tsx`

- `autoReadRoom` starts the editors' reading when a live-review quick grade
  arrives for a draft fingerprint the editors have not read, at most every
  `ROOM_READ_FLOOR_MS` (10 min, stored per folio), and only when a hosted
  client or BYOK provider exists.
- `runAnalysis(frontierOnly, quiet)` — a quiet run uses `isReviewing`, so the
  current grade stays on screen instead of the full-panel loader.
- The editors' notes survive later quick checks (`judges` carried forward);
  `judgesFingerprint` marks notes about an earlier version. A reading whose
  draft changed mid-run keeps its notes rather than discarding them.
- Automatic readings snapshot as `automatic` (5-minute spacing) so they cannot
  crowd manual checkpoints out of the 50-entry history; requested readings
  still force a `rubric` checkpoint.
- The Editors tab says `soon` / `reading…` instead of `0`.

### Research — `src/utils/background-research.ts`, `src/utils/research-candidates.ts` (new)

- Hosted writers without their own model: `claimCandidates` finds figures,
  attributed quotations, appeals to authority and dated events by rule;
  one batched Jev request (`candidateRequest`) confirms which need a source
  (Noul ≥ 0.6), with fiction instructed to ignore invented events.
- `ResearchIdleReason` (`waiting`, `too-short`, `no-provider`, `no-claims`,
  `covered`, `pass-done`) replaces the bare "Watching draft".
- Failed passes and failed claims retry on their own at 30 s, 2 min and
  10 min (`scheduleRetry`), then stop and leave the retry control.
- Each Deep trace row says what found / no match / failed means and offers
  Go to the claim.

## 2. Passage grounding and card meaning

- **Quotations** — `src/utils/quote-grounding.ts` (new). `extractQuotations`
  reads paired quotation marks and Markdown block quotes; `resolveQuotation`
  normalises typography, case and whitespace, follows `…` elisions within one
  paragraph, never crosses paragraphs, and breaks ties with the note's
  surrounding words (same paragraph only, stopwords removed). Ties stay
  `ambiguous`; missing text stays `unmatched`. `renderGroundedMarkdown` wraps
  resolved quotations as links after safe Markdown rendering. Links are
  re-resolved on `twyne:content` and again in the editor on click
  (`twyne:reveal-quote`, `findQuotationRange`). Used by the Cast panel notes
  and replies and the in-manuscript note card.
- **Relationship cards** — `flow-conductor.ts` asks a Choice alongside the echo
  Noul (`ECHO_RELATIONS`); shared vocabulary only suppresses the card. The card
  shows both passages and offers That's the connection / Not how I read it.
- **Settled notes** — `src/utils/note-decisions.ts` (new). Intentional / later
  per note, stored on this device (`note-decisions:<folioId>`). A decision
  stands while its anchor still resolves in the draft; `withoutSettled` drops
  repeat notes from the same editor in explicit and background passes, and
  `decisionsDigest` goes to the editors as context.

## 3. Versions — `src/utils/revision-history.ts`, `version-history-panel.tsx`

- `describeRevision` writes one sentence per comparison from the changes
  (rewrote / cut / added, and whose notes the rewrites reached).
- Changes are labelled Rewritten / Cut / New passage with Before and After.
- `notesTouchedBy` shows editor notes whose anchor was in the old passage and
  is gone from the new one — evidence the change reached the note, not proof
  it answered it.
- Optional intent on Save checkpoint (`RevisionSnapshot.intent`) names the
  checkpoint. Counts move under Size of the change.

## Answers to the brief's open questions

- **Cast cards / "further on as you read".** Cast cards are `PersonasPanel`
  notes (`personas-panel.tsx`); the "Further on in this piece" card is an
  `echo` flow item from `flow-conductor.ts`, rendered by `flow-surface.tsx`.
- **Editor review and the manual click.** The quick check never runs the
  editors; the click started their reading. It now starts on its own.
- **"Watching graph".** Research went idle silently when there was no
  provider, the draft was short, no claims were found or all were covered.
  Each is now a named state, and hosted writers have a provider path.
- **Jev's decisions.** Jev confirms echo relevance and relationship, hosted
  research claims, note quality gates, and the quick grade; the relationship
  label and the research claim rows surface those decisions.
- **Revision information.** Snapshots hold full HTML and Typst source, so
  passage-level before/after is exact; intent is now recorded when given, and
  note evidence is derived from stored editor notes.

## Not covered

- Unread markers for finished reviews.
- Rejected relationship readings are dismissed, not recorded as a rejected
  reading.
- Note decisions do not sync between devices.
- Manual screenshots for the Cast notes, echo card, Apparatus Deep trace and
  Version history predate these changes.

## Tests

`quote-grounding.test.ts`, `note-decisions.test.ts`,
`research-candidates.test.ts`, additions to `background-room.test.ts` and
`revision-history.test.ts`; `personas-markdown-wiring.test.ts` updated for the
grounded renderer.

1	=== getting-started
2	01 · At the desk Begin a piece Meet Morgan Vale, who has four thousand words about salt caravans and no idea what the essay is for. This manual follows that draft, Salt Roads, from a brief to a proof. Twyne is a writing desk with an editorial room attached. You write on the page. A small cast of editors reads in the margin, each with a different job, and nothing they say changes a word until you say so. Three habits make the room worth having: Say what the piece is for. The dossier holds the reader, the goal and the shape of the piece. Editors with a brief give better notes than editors guessing. Write first, read notes later. Your draft saves on this device as you type. The editors, the grade and the research read it on their own when you pause; there is nothing to press. The margin holds feedback beside the passage it belongs to, and waits until you look up. Revise on your own terms. Follow a note to its passage, argue with it, ask a different editor, or check the galley proof . Every change is yours to make or refuse. Go to the writing desk →
3	
4	=== dossier
5	02 · At the desk The dossier Morgan's first draft of Salt Roads was beautiful and pointless. The dossier is where you admit what a piece is supposed to do, so the editors can tell you whether it does it. Before the room opens, it asks a short series of questions. They feel like paperwork and they are the opposite: a dossier is the difference between an editor saying "this paragraph is weak" and an editor saying "this paragraph loses the reader you said you were writing for." Answer briefly and honestly. You can change any answer later. Ten sections, and what each is really asking: Working title. A name the room can use. It does not have to be the final one. Form. Essay, memo, chapter, dispatch, proposal. The shape sets expectations about length and manners. Reader. One real person, not a demographic. "A friend who hates travel writing" beats "general readers." Intent. What should be different in the reader when they finish? This is the question Morgan could not answer, and the one that fixed the essay. Voice. How it should feel to read, not just how it should sound. Non-negotiables. Sources to keep, jargon to avoid, the anecdote that must survive every cut. Landing. How you will know the draft has done its job. "The reader can picture the journey" is a test an editor can apply. Particulars. A few follow-up questions drawn from your own answers, to sharpen the softest ones. Prior material and References. Earlier drafts, field notes, links: anything the room should read, with a line on why it matters. The working copy grades each answer as you type, from vague to specific, and counts how many answers are carrying weight. A red mark is not a failure. It is the room telling you which question it would ask first. When the piece changes its mind: choose Refine the dossier at the desk and rewrite the answer that no longer holds. Each filing is kept as an edition, and the room reads the new one on its next pass.
6	
7	=== house
8	03 · At the desk The House & collections Salt Roads is the second of five coastal essays. Morgan is not going to type the same reader into five dossiers. The House is everything you would otherwise repeat: the reader you usually write for, the standards you always hold, the tone of the whole enterprise. A collection narrows that for a series. A folio is one manuscript with its own dossier. Context flows downward, and the most specific layer wins: House Your reusable audience, purpose and standards. Collection Shared context for a series of related pieces. Folio One manuscript, with its own dossier. A filled-in folio field overrides its collection, which overrides the House. Leave a field blank and it inherits. Working titles belong to each folio alone. Charter articles are the exception: they accumulate, so a House rule applies to every piece even when a collection adds rules of its own. Dossier The brief that tells the room what a piece is for. Charter Standards you require or prefer, at House, collection or folio level. "Every claim grounded in a concrete scene" is a Charter article. Edition A saved version of the dossier, with its source and reason. Amendment A proposed change to the dossier, usually offered from the margin. It takes effect only when you file it. Open the House to arrange collections, inspect what a folio inherited, and read the register of changes. "What the models read" is the assembled dossier and charter exactly as the editors receive it; each tool adds its own instructions and excerpts on top. The Engine room holds developer diagnostics and nothing a writer needs. If the editors start asking about something you never told them: look in the register. A collection default or an inherited Charter article is usually the answer, and the source stamp on each field says which.
9	
10	=== flow
11	04 · At the desk Writing in flow Morgan writes in long runs and resents anything that interrupts one. The room is built to wait. While you work, Twyne can bring comments, sources, books, records and echoes of your earlier writing into the margin, each beside the passage it concerns. Nothing pops up over the page. Hover or focus a marker to see what it connects to; select it to open the conversation in the same margin. A quieter page Automatic focus reads your typing cadence. When you have been writing steadily for a while, it quiets the room: new cards wait, controls recede, and the page is the only thing left. Pause, or reach for the room, and it comes back. You can also enter focus yourself with Zen in the manuscript status bar, and leave it with Esc . Help when you need it When a passage stalls, the margin may offer a single connection or a short way into the next sentence. These are offers, not corrections; ignore them and they go away. If what you are writing drifts from the dossier, the room may propose an amendment. It never rewrites the brief behind your back. Why two passages are side by side Halfway through Salt Roads, Morgan writes about the salt merchant's ledger, and a card appears: Earlier in this piece. Unpaid promise. The opening said the ledger would explain the road, and nothing has explained it yet. The card names the relationship (an unpaid promise, a tension, an echo, a repetition, or the same subject) and says in a sentence why it matters. It shows both passages; select either to go to it. A relationship is a reading, not a fault. Some promises are meant to stay open. Choose That's the connection if the reading is right, or Not how I read it to set the card aside for good. A card matched only on shared words says so, rather than pretending to know more. Your controls: Automatic review, margin tools, automatic focus and cover lookups each have their own switch in the review controls. The desk learns your timing and preferences on this device. Cover lookups are the one feature here that talks to the outside world: they send book or record titles to external catalogues.
12	
13	=== the-piece
14	05 · At the desk The piece Some problems only show up across the whole draft: the voice that shifts, the name spelled two ways, the character who vanishes for a chapter. Useful without a model The piece runs on this device, with no model and no cost. It watches first-person stance, similar names, and the conventions your draft mostly follows: spelling, small numbers, quotation marks, dashes and list punctuation. It also maps where each recurring name appears across the headed sections. A finding is a pattern worth a look. Whether it is a problem is your call. Choose Stance, Names, Style or Presence to see that lens on the page. Open a finding for its passages and the actions it offers. On a narrow screen the desk sits below the writing area, and Close gives the space back to the draft. Zen hides it while you write. Know what the score means The ≈ sign marks an estimate. Consistency can move as you revise, because local rules re-count; that movement is not a new editorial opinion. Score details separates the measures made by rule from those made by review. An overall estimate appears at about 150 words. Confirm with a full read asks for a fresh editorial reading of the current draft. It needs automatic review switched on, at least 500 words, and a signed-in model service. The desk says so when a request cannot run. Edit again afterwards and the score becomes an estimate until the new draft has been read. Your choices stay yours. Fixes change only the listed passages, and Undo reverses them. A deliberate exception stays with the folio on this device. Above 80,000 characters the desk pauses these checks and asks you to divide the work into folios.
15	
16	=== writing-instruments
17	06 · At the desk Writing instruments A sentence that is almost right. A paragraph that sounds like one you wrote earlier. A scene with no sound in it. Each gets a tool that opens beside the words, not instead of them. Select text in the manuscript and the tools that fit it appear. A single word offers Alternatives. A passage offers Rework, with Hear it read, Threads, Scene bench and Task desk under More. The Compositor also opens Task desk from Review. Close a tool, or press Escape, and the page is back. Work on a whole sentence Morgan's opening line has been rewritten nine times. Sentence bench keeps the working wording at the top with Use this wording beside it. Rewrite lists complete earlier wordings, rule-based changes and model alternatives, each with its word-count change. Choose one to make it the working wording, or Compare to keep the original alongside. Hover or keyboard-focus a candidate to preview it in place on the page. How these were checked shows the grammar status and any meaning the check could not verify. Undo restores the edit. Words offers bundled thesaurus choices shown inside the full sentence, and underlines words you have already used in the paragraph. A synonym can change the meaning, so read the sentence again. With the Words in context pack installed, On-device alternatives adds local word predictions. Likely is not the same as right. Place shows where else the sentence could sit, with the sentences on either side. Read each arrangement before choosing Move here; the reasons come from local rules and no model has judged them. Hear reads the sentence before, the working wording and the sentence after through your narration player, using a downloaded local voice or your voice service. Follow a thread Threads pairs exact sentences from the manuscript that may be talking to each other. Hover or keyboard-focus a pair to mark both passages; choose a sentence to go to it. Local checks find repeated wording, shared vocabulary and possible references. A relation stays unverified until the judgement service has read it; a model reading names its source and shows how sure it is. For an exact repeat, you can remove either occurrence as one undoable edit. Repetition is sometimes the point, so leaving both is always an option. If the passage changes, reopen the instrument before trusting its earlier reading. Follow an entity through the piece In the instrument desk, choose Entities. Select a name candidate to see every mention across the sections and read the source passages. The index is local and literal: it can include places or ordinary capitalised words, and a candidate is not a confirmed character. Spelling variants are grouped by a local rule. Choose a reading, then Read with judgement model to inspect relationships by section, compare a named attribute such as the colour of a coat, or try blind dialogue attribution. The blind reading hides speaker tags and is allowed to answer Unknown. Every result keeps its exact evidence and full distribution. A possible contradiction is a lead to chase, and a model's confidence is not a grade for your characterisation. Read paragraphs; keep your choices Open Paragraph readings in The piece to see each paragraph's scores and narrating tense. Local English cues and Jev readings are labelled separately so you know which is which. Inspect distributions and context shows the exact paragraph behind a reading, including a split or uncertain result. These readings stand apart from the whole-piece grade and its estimate. Keeping a deliberate style or name exception saves the existing uses in the folio's Charter. New drift can still be flagged. Check these again removes the exception. A save notice tells you if the choice could only be kept on this device. Invite an editor into the work Sentence bench, each Threads pair and Scene bench offer Ask the room . Your judgement model, Jev when selected, reads the passage, your working proposal and the tool's question, then chooses the editor most likely to help. It may choose no one. You can also pick an editor yourself. The chosen editor replies in Marginalia, with their portrait and name above the critique. The saved question keeps the original passage separate from any unapplied wording or scene idea, so the editor knows what is on the page and what is only proposed. The reply uses your writing model and your provider settings govern the charge. If the source changes before the request is filed, reopen the instrument. The manuscript stays yours. Leave a question at the Task desk Some questions need more than a margin note: "does the ford scene contradict the field notes?" Choose Writing review or Research selected account resources, confirm the reference passage, and describe what would help. For research, enable resource access in Account sources and choose up to three texts. The task reads those and only those; it does not search the open web. Sign in with Not Organic and sync the folio before queueing. Once your account accepts the request, the work continues on the server after you close the tab, using your hosted model and account credit. Come back to this folio's Task desk for the status, the result, the saved passage and the source excerpts. If the draft has moved on, read the earlier context before acting on the answer. You can cancel unfinished work. A request already with a provider may still finish and incur its charge, but its result is discarded. Mark a returned result Useful or Not useful and add a comment; the feedback is saved with the task. Results are proposals, never edits. Keep a few tools on your device From Task desk, choose On-device tools. Passage connections, Words in context and Say it are separate English-language packs, each with its download size shown. Download & load is an explicit choice, with Stop download and Remove pack beside it. Model files come from Hugging Face and the shared runtime from jsDelivr; keep the page open for the first load. Once installed, these tools use no account credit, and your passages and recordings never leave the device. Passage connections compares nearby passages you choose. Its similarity score is an invitation to read closer; it does not prove a repetition or a missing transition. For Say it , install the speech pack, select a sentence, then record up to a minute or pick an audio clip. Review the transcript before using it as a candidate wording. Browsers can clear or evict storage, so a pack may one day need downloading again. See what a scene gives you Scene bench takes stock of a passage by sense: place, time, light, sound, movement and pressure, each backed by exact quotes from your selection. The local English scan names the cue it found. A cue it did not find may still be there in a form it does not recognise. An optional judgement reading can select evidence and assess pressure; its service and cost appear before you ask for it. Hear the passage uses your narration player. Ideas stay beside the evidence. Under Try a detail, save a sound or an image you want to try without touching the manuscript. Image, sound and motion briefs keep those additions clearly separate from the original passage, ready to paste into another tool. See it as a reader might can sketch a picture of the scene, but scene pictures are off until you enable them in Settings, because generating one spends credit. Above 12,000 characters or 64 sentences the bench asks for a shorter selection.
18	
19	=== room
20	07 · The editorial room Your editors Five resident voices, each reading for something different. No single editor is right about everything, which is rather the point of having five. You will come to know them by their faces. The same portraits accompany each editor's critiques, margin replies and rubric readings, so a glance tells you whether it was the sceptic or the copy chief who objected. A custom editor without a portrait signs with their initials. From any writing instrument, Ask the room brings one of them into the question you are already working on. They read without being asked Morgan never convenes the room. Once a draft reaches 500 words, the editors read it on their own the first time Morgan pauses. After that they come back whenever about 200 words are new or rewritten and the page has been quiet for a minute. A rewrite counts as much as new material, so tightening the harbour section brings fresh notes. They read only the paragraphs that changed, along with a sketch of how the draft has been moving. Those notes arrive marked in passing, lighter than the notes you ask for. There are at least five minutes between readings and a limit per session, because this spends model calls without a click. Get notes is still there when you want the whole room now. Read as I write, in the room settings, turns the automatic reading off. Every quotation leads somewhere When Marguerite quotes three lines of Salt Roads in one note, each quotation is underlined and goes to its own passage, not to the first one. Twyne matches the words literally. It ignores curly quotes, capitals and spacing, and follows a quotation with an ellipsis in it. If the same phrase appears twice, the words around the quotation in the note decide which one is meant. A quotation that could be either, or that is no longer in the draft because Morgan has since rewritten it, gets a dotted underline instead of a link. Hover over it to see why. Twyne would rather leave a quotation unplaced than send you to the wrong sentence, and it checks again every time the draft changes. Meant as written, or for later The abrupt ending of the ferry scene is deliberate, and Mlle. Sceptique will not stop pointing it out. Choose intentional on her note. Choose later for a note you agree with but will deal with after this draft. Either way, that editor will not raise the same passage again until its words change. The settled note steps back on the page, and selecting the label again undoes the decision. Decisions are kept on this device. Arrange your room Custom editors: Visit the Room of Editors to add, edit or reorder the cast. An editor needs a name, a role and a description of how they talk; the more specific the description, the more consistently the model stays in character. Morgan's Route Reader exists because nobody else in the room cared about distances. Changing the model Each editor is only as good as the model reading for them. A careful, precise model makes Mlle. Sceptique sharper. A warmer one makes Sœur Encourageante more generous. In Preferences you can assign different models to different jobs, and the room adapts.
21	
22	=== rubric
23	08 · The editorial room The galley proof Salt Roads got a B. That is not information. The reasons under the grade are. The static features are the part of the proof that never guesses: sentence length distribution, type-token ratio, citation density, paragraph shape. They are computed on this device, cost nothing and call nothing. They give you a cold, honest picture of the draft's mechanics, and nothing at all about whether it is any good. Quick check When the signed-in service is available, the default check makes one typed judgement request against your enabled criteria, custom ones included. You get a grade without separate verdicts from the five editors. If the quick check is unavailable, Twyne falls back to the room reading. The editors' reading The grade arrives on its own. Once the draft has 500 words and you pause, Twyne runs the quick check. The editors then read the new version themselves, at most once every ten minutes, and the grade stays on screen while they work. Until they finish, the Editors tab says soon rather than showing a zero. Choose Ask them now there if you would rather not wait. When the quick check refreshes after an edit, the editors' notes stay, marked as being about an earlier version until they read the new one. Each editor gives a score and a rationale, and the places where they disagree are usually where the revision is. This path combines editorial verdicts with the static features. Its Target Fit check caps the shape scores when a piece misses the audience or purpose in its dossier, because a beautifully built essay for the wrong reader is still the wrong essay. What the letters mean: A range. Publishable or nearly so. Polish. B range. A solid draft with clear, fixable problems. This is where Salt Roads sits. C range. Doing the work, but a real pass is still needed. D to F range. The important next pass is still ahead. Use the rationale, not the letter: read the explanation beside each criterion and hold it against your own purpose. The rubric is one more reading of the draft. You decide which of its complaints deserve a revision.
24	
25	=== marginalia
26	09 · The editorial room Margin conversations Every argument about a passage happens next to the passage. Your notes, the editors' notes, and the replies between them. Select any passage and choose Comment to leave a note in the margin. Notes belong to the folio and travel with it. Each one can hold replies, and Ask an editor invites a particular voice into the thread when you want a second opinion on your own doubt. Select a passage marker to unfold its thread beside the manuscript. Reply, ask an editor or resolve it there. One conversation is in the foreground at a time; on a narrow screen its card stays anchored to the passage. Press Esc to close it. A reply you have not sent survives switching threads during the visit, but not a reload, so send it or lose it.
27	
28	=== apparatus
29	10 · The editorial room Research & citations The 1911 survey, the tide table, the book Morgan keeps paraphrasing. The Apparatus notices them and keeps them in order. The Apparatus does three things: finds sources, keeps them, and cites them. As you write it recognises DOIs, URLs, ISBNs and author-year references in the text. You can also search by query; the panel returns a shortlist with title, author, publisher and a snippet. Save what matters to the bibliography and ignore the rest. The bibliography is formatted in the style you choose, MLA, APA or Chicago, and switches instantly when an editor changes their mind. Copy the whole list to the clipboard in one go. Research that runs itself Morgan does not ask for sources. A short while after Morgan stops typing, the Apparatus reads the draft and picks out what a careful reader would want backed up: the figure about the salt trade, the line quoted from the 1911 survey, the year the harbour closed. It searches for each one and files what it finds under the claim that prompted it. With your own model configured, that model picks the claims. Signed in without one, Twyne finds them in the text and Jev confirms which really need a source. In fiction, invented events are left alone. The panel always says what it is doing: reading the draft, searching, or why it is idle. It might be waiting for a pause, the draft might be too short, there might be no claims that need a source, or every claim may already be covered. Each claim in Deep trace explains its result. Found means sources are on file, so check that they support your wording. No match means the search ran and found nothing, so the claim may need softer wording or a source of your own. Failed means the search broke, which is not the same as finding nothing. Twyne tries a failed search again on its own after thirty seconds, two minutes and ten minutes; retry is there if you want it sooner. Go to the claim shows the sentence in the manuscript. The full Apparatus lives at /apparatus . The citation tab in the right panel shows a quick view of what has been detected without leaving the page.

31	=== account-and-live
32	11 · The editorial room Your account & Live A name for the editors to address you by, and a way to talk to one out loud when typing is too slow. Sign in with Not Organic to carry your account, hosted credits and plan across devices. Your name and picture identify you in the room; your email stays in private account settings and appears nowhere else. You can keep writing locally without ever signing in. Talk opens a voice conversation with an editor, from the compositor, from one of their comments, or from the narration player. Live shows captions, lets you mute the microphone, and can find passages or propose edits as you speak. A proposed edit waits for your approval before it touches the manuscript. Switching folios ends the conversation. Captions and microphone audio are not saved. Live needs a Pro plan or available Twyne welcome credit. A conversation reserves up to $0.50; delegated language requests cap at $0.05 each on top. The voice desk shows these limits before you start, which is why it is worth reading.

34	=== manuscript-tools
35	12 · Your work Manuscript & source tools Headings, tables, a footnote, a pull quote set just so. The page is a real page, and when it is not enough there is the source underneath it. Move through the manuscript Type / at the start of a block to open the insert menu. The outline jumps between headings, and dragging a heading's section handle moves that section with everything under it in one undoable edit. Find and Replace understands whole words, case and regular expressions. Tables and images Tables come with a size picker, captions, row and column tools, cell shading, alignment, borders and reusable visual presets. Images can be dropped, pasted or chosen from disk; select one to set its alt text, caption, alignment, width and see its upload status. Online images are stored with the folio. Deliberately offline work keeps an inline copy instead. Source and proof The Typst workspace lets you edit the source directly and read a paginated proof. A source draft recovers on this device after a reload. Apply a valid draft to update the folio; if another device has changed the base in the meantime, resolve that conflict first. An invalid draft is never applied and stays there for you to fix. Shape the page Notes and equations Inline and display equations accept LaTeX and render on this device. 37	=== folios
38	13 · Your work Folios, export & publishing One piece per folio. Salt Roads, its outline and a scratch file of cut paragraphs share a collection and nothing else. Folios are separate documents with separate dossiers. Switch between them from the drawer. Each keeps its own word count, last-updated time and, if you want, its own layout settings. Export a folio as Markdown, standalone HTML, plain text, PDF, Word, Typst source, or a full Twyne backup: a JSON file with the brief, the folios and their content. All of it is under File in the masthead. Share publishes a public reading view of a folio. Anyone with the link can read it and nobody can edit it. Unpublish takes it down at once. Publish to your PDS by connecting Bluesky or another ATProto provider in the Share dialog. That connection is separate from your Not Organic sign-in. Twyne files a Standard.site publication and document in your own repository, serves a verifiable public reading page, and updates the same record when you publish again. Unpublishing removes the document from your PDS. PDF (Typst) compiles the manuscript on this device with bundled fonts, equations and diagrams included, and reports any source or asset problem before the export. You can also download the .typ source. Private editorial annotations are stripped from the exported copy; your saved source keeps them. What a revision did Twyne saves checkpoints on its own as you write, and whenever you ask for a grade. Version history describes each comparison in a sentence, written from the changes themselves: Rewrote three passages and cut one. The changes reach passages Marguerite had notes on. Each changed passage is labelled Rewritten, Cut or New passage, with the before and after text together. When a rewrite reaches a passage an editor had a note on, the note is shown beside it. That shows the change reached the passage, not that it answered the note. Save checkpoint takes an optional line saying what the revision was for, such as "pay off the ledger promise", and that line names the checkpoint afterwards. The word and passage counts are still there under Size of the change. Restore always saves the current draft first.

40	=== byok
41	14 · Your work Bring your own key Morgan already pays for a model and would like the editors to use it. Three steps, once. Add a provider. In Preferences , switch on Bring Your Own Key and add an OpenAI, Anthropic or Google key. For anything else, Groq, Together, Rivet, a local server, choose the OpenAI-compatible option and give it the base URL. Test the key. Choose Test key on the provider card. A successful check proves the key reaches the model list, and lets you refresh the models you can pick from. Pick models per feature. The per-feature grid assigns different models to the room, the rubric and the other tools. Spend the expensive model where reading quality matters and leave the rest on something cheaper. Supported providers: OpenAI Anthropic Google OpenAI-compatible (Groq, Together, Rivet, local servers, …) If a connection fails: check the provider and key in Preferences and test again. The desk keeps working while a provider is down; only the editors go quiet.

43	=== privacy
44	15 · Your work Privacy & your data The manuscript is yours. Here is exactly where it goes, and where it does not. API keys are saved in your browser's IndexedDB. A remote BYOK request passes through Twyne's server relay, which forwards your key and the request to the provider you chose and keeps neither. Local model endpoints are called directly. Drafts and folios are saved in your browser profile. Signing out does not erase that local copy. Signing in to an account that has no cloud snapshot can sync the existing local work into it, and signed-in sync is what gives you the same work on another device. AI calls send draft text to whichever model is reading. With your own key, that is the provider you chose, through the relay for remote endpoints. Hosted calls go through Convex and Not Organic, where provider processing and content-logging consent are managed. Published pieces are the only ones anyone else can read. Nothing becomes public until you publish it. Sharing and collaboration grant exactly the access you choose, through their own controls.

Recipe that worked on 2026-10-17 for verifying editor UI changes without the Convex backend:

Instead, seed like `e2e/instruments.e2e.ts` `seed()`: route `/api/auth/` to `null`, visit a routed blank page, `import("/src/utils/idb.ts")` in page context, then call saveFoliosToIdb / saveFolioContentToIdb / saveActiveFolioIdToIdb (+ `signin-toast-dismissed` meta, `twyne:editor:view:v1` with zenMode false).
